q: 101. The under drainage system in a rapid sand filters .............
options: receives and collects the filtered water
allows back washing for cleaning the filter
explain: In rapid sand filters, the under-drainage system is multifunctional: it collects filtered water during the run and distributes high-pressure wash water and air during the cleaning (backwash) cycle.

q: 102. The slow sand filters should be cleaned if the loss of head becomes more than .............
explain: When the head loss reaches approximately 0.7 to 1.2 meters (roughly 70% to 80% of the sand bed depth), the filter is considered 'clogged' and requires scraping.

q: 103. After cleaning the slow sand filter, the filtered water should not be used for a period of .............
explain: Scraping removes the biological layer (Schmutzdecke). It takes 24 to 48 hours for this layer to reform and restore the filter's bacterial removal efficiency.

q: 104. Cleaning period for slow sand filter is taken as .............
explain: Slow sand filters have a long filter run, typically requiring cleaning only once every 1 to 3 months depending on raw water turbidity.

q: 105. Rate of filtration of a slow sand filter ranges from .............
explain: Slow sand filters operate at a very low rate, usually between 100 to 200 liters per hour per square meter of filter area.

q: 106. Slow sand filter is efficient to remove the bacteria from the raw water to an extent of .............
explain: Due to the Schmutzdecke (biological layer), slow sand filters are exceptionally good at removing bacteria, often achieving 98% to 99% removal.

q: 107. Slow sand filter is more efficient for the removal of .............
explain: While they remove some turbidity and odour, the primary technical advantage of slow sand filters is their superior bacterial removal capability.

q: 108. In rapid sand filter .............
options: raw water from the sources is supplied
raw water passed through coagulation tank is supplied
explain: Rapid sand filters cannot handle high turbidity alone; they must be preceded by coagulation and sedimentation to be effective.

q: 109. The yield of a rapid sand filter is ............. to that of slow sand filter.
explain: Rapid sand filters have filtration rates (3000-6000 L/h/m²) that are roughly 30 times higher than slow sand filters (100-200 L/h/m²).

q: 110. An arrangement for back washing is provided in .............
explain: Backwashing (reversing water flow to expand the sand bed) is the standard method for cleaning rapid sand filters.

q: 111. In a rapid sand filter, the filter head varies from .............
explain: Rapid sand filters are designed to operate with a head loss of up to 3 to 4 meters before they require backwashing.

q: 112. Cleaning of rapid sand filters is done by .............
options: scraping the top layer of filter media
explain: Unlike slow sand filters which are scraped, rapid sand filters are cleaned by forceful backwashing with water and sometimes air.

q: 113. Cleaning period for a rapid sand filter is taken as .............
explain: Because they operate at much higher rates, rapid sand filters clog quickly and typically need cleaning every 1 to 3 days.

q: 114. rapid sand filter can remove bacteria upto an extent of .............
explain: Rapid sand filters are less efficient at bacterial removal (80-90%) than slow sand filters because they lack the biological 'dirty skin' layer.

q: 115. Rapid sand filter can remove turbidity from water upto an extend of .............
explain: Rapid sand filters are designed to handle and remove higher levels of turbidity compared to slow sand filters, provided pre-treatment is correct.

q: 116. pressure filters are not used for treating municipal water supplies, because .............
options: the rate of filtration is high
the overall plant capacity is small
they are efficient in the removal of turbidity and bacteria
explain: Pressure filters are compact but not scalable for massive municipal demands; their design is better suited for smaller, localized applications.

q: 117. Pressure filters are best suited for .............
explain: Due to their high rate and enclosed design, they are ideal for swimming pools, industrial sites, and small colonies.

q: 118. The process of killing pathogenic bacteria from water is called .............
explain: Disinfection specifically targets the destruction of disease-causing organisms to make water safe for consumption.

q: 119. The most commonly used disinfectant for drinking water throughout the world is .............
explain: Chlorine is used globally because it is effective, provides a residual effect in pipes, and is relatively inexpensive.

q: 120. The ideal method of disinfection of swimming pool water is by .............
explain: Ozone is a very powerful oxidant that leaves no unpleasant 'chlorine smell' or taste, making it ideal for high-end swimming pools.

q: 121. The amount of residual chlorine in treated water is determined by the .............
explain: Orthotolidine is the common field test, while Iodometric and Amperometric titration are used for more precise laboratory measurements.

q: 122. The time of contact for chlorination should be at least .............
explain: Chlorine requires a 'contact time' (usually 20-30 minutes) to successfully react with and kill microorganisms.

q: 123. The treatment of water with only chlorine is known as .............
explain: Plain chlorination is the process of adding chlorine to raw water that has not received any other treatment (like filtration or sedimentation).

q: 124. Pre-chlorination .............
explain: Adding chlorine at the start of the treatment process helps oxidize organic matter, improving the performance of subsequent stages.

q: 125. The prevent formation of crystalline hydrates of 'Ice' of chlorine, the chlorine supply cylinders are kept at a temperature from .............
explain: Maintaining a moderate temperature prevents the chlorine from forming solid hydrates which could block valves and pipes.

q: 126. Crystalline hydrates of 'Ice' of chlorine are formed at a temperature of .............
explain: At temperatures below 9.6°C, chlorine can form solid yellow crystals (chlorine ice) in the presence of water.

q: 127. The apparatus used for feeding chlorine into water is called .............
explain: A chlorinator is a mechanical device designed to regulate and inject precise amounts of chlorine gas or liquid into a water stream.

q: 128. When the chlorine is added beyond the break point, the process of treating the water is known as .............
explain: Super-chlorination involves adding high doses of chlorine to effectively treat heavily polluted water or during epidemics.

q: 129. The process of removing excess chlorine from water is called .............
explain: De-chlorination is necessary when the residual chlorine level is too high for safe or pleasant consumption.

q: 130. The process of dechlorination is followed by .............
explain: After super-chlorination and de-chlorination, a small 'post-chlorination' dose is often added to maintain a safe residual in the network.

q: 131. The amount of chlorine used for plain chlorination of water is about .............
explain: Plain chlorination typically requires around 0.5 mg/L (ppm) to achieve proper disinfection in relatively clean raw water.

q: 132. The most commonly used chemical for dechlorination of water is .............
explain: Sodium thiosulphate is the standard chemical used to neutralize excess chlorine rapidly.

q: 133. In orthotolodine test, safe residual for drinking water is indicated by .............
explain: A lemon-yellow color in an OT test indicates a safe residual chlorine level of approximately 0.1 to 0.2 ppm.

q: 134. Bleaching power is .............
explain: Bleaching powder is chemically known as Calcium Hypochlorite, $Ca(OCl)_2$.

q: 135. The percentage of chlorine in fresh bleaching power is .............
explain: Commercial 'fresh' bleaching powder usually contains about 30% to 35% available chlorine.

q: 136. The temporary hardness in water is caused due to the salts like .............
explain: Temporary (carbonate) hardness is caused by bicarbonates and carbonates of calcium and magnesium.

q: 137. The permanent hardness in water is caused due to the salts like .............
explain: Non-carbonate (permanent) hardness is caused by chlorides, nitrates, and sulphates of calcium and magnesium.

q: 138. The temporary hardness due to calcium bicarbonates can be removed by .............
explain: Boiling causes bicarbonates to decompose into insoluble carbonates, which then precipitate out of the water.

q: 139. The permanent hardness of water can be removed by .............
explain: The Zeolite (base-exchange) process is highly effective at removing both temporary and permanent hardness.

q: 140. By lime soda process, hardness can be reduced to less than .............
explain: While Zeolite reaches zero hardness, the chemical Lime-Soda process typically reduces it to about 30-50 ppm.

q: 141. The lime soda process of water softening .............
options: is suitable for turbid and acidic water
explain: The Lime-Soda process provides several side benefits, including disinfection (due to high pH) and assisting in coagulation.
Natural or synthetic zeolites are complex compounds of Sodium Aluminum Silicate used for ion exchange.

q: 143. In zeolite process .............
options: water of varying quality can be treated
ferrous and manganese from water are removed
explain: The Zeolite process is clean (no sludge), versatile, and removes other metallic ions besides hardness-causing ones.

q: 144. Zeolite process is also known as .............
explain: The terms 'Base Exchange' and 'Cation Exchange' are synonymous with the Zeolite softening process.

q: 145. A sluice valve, in water distribution system, is used to .............
options: protect the pipe against negative pressure
regulate the flow of water through the pipe
prevent water of flow back in the opposite direction
explain: Sluice valves (Gate valves) are used to isolate sections of the network or regulate the flow by opening/closing the pipe path.

q: 146. A reflux valve, in water distribution system is used to .............
options: protect the pipe against negative pressure
regulate the flow of water through the pipe
prevent water of flow back in the opposite direction
explain: A Reflux valve allows water to flow in one direction only, preventing backflow into pumps or reservoirs.

q: 147. A reflux valve is also known as .............
explain: Check valve and non-return valve are common alternative names for a reflux valve.

q: 148. A scour valve, in a water distribution system, is provided at .............
explain: Scour valves (Blow-off valves) are placed at low points to drain the pipe and remove accumulated silt/sediment.

q: 149. If the level of sources of water is higher than that of the place of consumption, the system adopted for supplying water is .............
explain: A gravity system uses the natural elevation difference to move water without the need for mechanical pumps.

q: 150. The hydrants are used for tapping water from mains for .............
explain: Fire hydrants provide high-volume access to municipal water for emergency use and maintenance tasks like street or sewer flushing.

q: 151. The minimum size of as fire hydrants is
explain: For effective fire fighting, a minimum diameter of 10 cm is generally required to ensure sufficient water discharge and pressure.

q: 152. The valve provided on the suction pipe in a tube well is
explain: A reflux valve (also known as a check valve or foot valve in suction) is used to prevent the backflow of water when the pump stops, keeping the pump primed.

q: 153. A pressure relief valve is provided to
options: the back flow, when the pump is stopped
prevent the increase of pressure after certain safe limit
explain: Pressure relief valves are safety devices designed to open and release fluid when the pressure exceeds a predefined limit, protecting the pipe from bursting.

q: 154. A valve which allows the water to flow in one direction but prevents its flows in the reverse direction, is known as
explain: Reflux valves (check valves) are automatic valves that permit flow in only one direction and close automatically to prevent backflow.

q: 155. The type of joint to be used in pipes depends upon the
explain: Pipe joint selection must consider the pipe material, the pressure it will sustain, and the stability or movement of the ground/supports.

q: 156. The plain ends of cast iron pipes are joined by
explain: Dresser coupling is a mechanical joint used to connect plain-ended pipes, offering flexibility and ease of assembly.

q: 157. The pipe joint commonly used in pumping stations is
explain: Flanged joints are preferred in pumping stations and treatment plants because they are easy to assemble and disassemble for maintenance.

q: 158. In order to control the flow of water through pipes, a ............... is provided.
explain: Gate valves (also known as sluice valves) are used to start or stop the flow of water; they are used as isolation valves rather than for throttling.

q: 159. In order to prevent water to flow back opposite direction, we shall use a
explain: Reflux valves are used specifically to ensure water flows in the intended direction only, preventing reversal.

q: 160. The capacity of the pumps is normally expressed as
explain: Pump capacity (discharge) can be expressed in various units depending on the scale, including L/min, m³/day, or L/hr.

q: 161. For an area developed in haphazard way, the types of layout for the distribution of pipes is
explain: The dead-end system (tree system) is used for unplanned/haphazard cities as it follows the irregular road patterns and is cheap.

q: 162. The suitable layout of a distribution system for well-planned cities is
explain: The ring (circular) system is ideal for well-planned cities where the main pipe follows the periphery, ensuring constant pressure and supply from two directions.

q: 163. For a city or town with roads of rectangular pattern, the type of layout used for the distribution of pipes
explain: The grid-iron system is used where roads are rectangular (grid pattern), minimizing dead ends and ensuring water reaches every point.

q: 164. Garbage is a
explain: Garbage refers to decomposable solid/dry waste, specifically organic matter from kitchens and food handling.

q: 165. The water from kitchens, bathrooms, wash basins is called
explain: Sullage is waste water from households that does not contain human excreta (from baths, kitchens, etc.).

q: 166. The quantity of liquid waste which flows in sewers during rainy seasons is called
explain: Storm sewage (or storm water) refers to the runoff generated by rainfall during the rainy season.

q: 167. A sewer which receives storm water, surface run-off and sewage is called a
explain: A combined sewer carries both sanitary sewage (domestic/industrial) and storm water in a single pipe.

q: 168. A sewer which receives sewage from the collection system and conducts it to a point of final disposal is called a
explain: The outfall sewer is the final section of the sewer line that carries the collected sewage to the treatment plant or disposal point.

q: 169. A pipe conveying sewage from the plumbing system of a single building to a common sewer is called
explain: House sewers (or house drains) connect the building's plumbing to the lateral or public sewer.

q: 170. A sewer which receives discharge of a number of houses sewers called a
explain: Lateral sewers collect waste from individual house sewers and discharge them into branch or main sewers.

q: 171. A sewer which gets discharge from two or more main sewers is called
explain: A trunk sewer is a large pipe that receives sewage from multiple main sewers for transport to a treatment plant.

q: 172. The self cleaning velocity, in order to prevent settling down of sewage in a large sewer is
explain: A velocity of approximately 0.75 m/s is required to ensure that solids do not settle at the bottom of the sewer pipes.

q: 173. The method in which different types of refuse are collected, carried and disposed off separately is called
explain: The conservancy system (dry system) involves manual collection and separate disposal of different wastes (human excreta vs. garbage).

q: 174. The water carriage sewage system removes
explain: Water carriage systems use water as the medium to transport domestic, industrial, and often storm water through underground pipes.

q: 175. A combined system will be favourable when
options: the sewers are to be laid in rocks
the topography is flat necessitating deep excavation
the locality to be served had narrow streets
explain: Flat topography makes a combined system more favorable because laying two separate pipes would require twice the deep, expensive excavation.

q: 176. A separate system will be favourable when
options: the sewers are to be laid in rocks
the topography is flat necessitating deep excavation
explain: Separate systems are generally better for hilly terrain or rocky areas where storm water can be easily diverted into natural channels, or when budget for large combined pipes is limited.

q: 177. The sanitation system in which a small portion of storm water enters sanitary sewers is known as
explain: In a partially separate system, sewage and storm water from roofs/pavements go into one pipe, while general street storm water goes into another.

q: 178. The storm sewers are essentially required to
options: avoid creation of unfavourable healthy conditions
improve the general appearance of the city
dispose off the first washings of early showers
explain: Storm sewers prevent flooding, remove dirty 'first wash' water from roads, and help maintain city hygiene during monsoon.

q: 179. According to Fanning's formula, the quantity of storm water (Q) in litres per seconds is given by
explain: Fanning's empirical formula for discharge estimation is $Q = CA^{5/6}$ where A is the area.

q: 180. The internal diameter of the sewer should not be less than
explain: Standard engineering practice (and many codes) dictates a minimum diameter of 150mm (15cm) to prevent frequent clogging.

q: 181. For house drainage and lateral connection, we shall use
explain: Vitrified stone ware (clay) pipes are preferred for domestic drainage due to their resistance to corrosion and cost-effectiveness.

q: 182. Egg-shaped sewers are generally used for
explain: While best for combined systems to maintain velocity during low flow, they can technically be used in any system.

q: 183. The cross-section recommended for separate system of sewerage is
explain: Circular sewers are the most efficient and economical choice for separate systems where flow remains relatively constant.

q: 184. An egg-shaped cross-section of a sewer
options: is economical than circular cross section
is more stable than circular cross section
provides self cleaning velocity in dry weather
explain: The hydraulic radius of the egg shape at low flow levels ensures higher velocity compared to a circular pipe, maintaining self-cleaning conditions during dry weather.

q: 185. For the sewers of diameter less than 600 mm, the type of joint preferred is
explain: Spigot and socket joints are standard for smaller diameter pipes, providing easy alignment and sealing.

q: 186. For the sewers of diameter more than 600 mm, the type of joint preferred is
explain: Collar joints are generally used for large diameter concrete pipes (over 600mm) for structural stability.

q: 187. Manholes are, generally, located
options: at all junctions of main and branch sewers
explain: Manholes are essential maintenance access points required whenever the pipe path, slope, or size changes, and at junctions.

q: 188. For large sewers, the maximum distance between manholes should be
explain: In larger, walkable sewers, manholes can be placed further apart, with 300m being a common maximum limit for cleaning operations.

q: 189. The lower portion of a manhole is known as
explain: The working chamber is the lower section of the manhole where a person can stand to perform inspections or cleaning.

q: 190. The minimum diameter of a manholes cover should be
explain: A 50cm diameter is the standard minimum to allow a worker to pass through comfortably.

q: 191. Manholes on sewer lines are provided for
explain: The primary purpose of a manhole is to provide access for periodic cleaning and removal of blockages.

q: 192. A drop manhole is provided if
options: a sewer drops from a height
a branch sewer discharges into main sewer at a higher level
explain: A drop manhole is specifically used when the vertical difference between the branch sewer and the main sewer is more than 0.6m.

q: 193. The equipment used for checking the levels of the sewer inverts is
explain: Boning rods (along with sight rails) are traditional tools used during excavation to ensure the sewer pipe is laid at the correct gradient.

q: 194. A good trap should
options: provide an adequate water seal at all times
explain: The water seal is the most critical feature of a trap, preventing foul gases from entering the building while allowing waste water to flow.

q: 195. Ventilation of house drainage is required to
options: relive the pressure of foul gases
dilute the foul air in the drain
reduce the obnoxious effect of foul air
explain: Ventilation prevents air pressure buildup that could break water seals and helps keep the drainage system free of foul odors.

q: 196. In one pipe system of plumbing
options: the main pipe is connected directly to the drainage system
all the traps are fully ventilated
explain: In a one-pipe system, a single vertical pipe carries both soil (waste from toilets) and waste (from sinks/baths), requiring extensive ventilation for safety.

q: 197. In one pipe system of plumbing, waste water is carried away from
explain: Waste water (sullage) from all these fixtures is collected into the same main pipe as human waste in this system.

q: 198. The pipe through which liquid waste carrying human excreta flows, is called
explain: A soil pipe is the plumbing component designed specifically to carry discharge from WCs (water closets) or urinals.

q: 199. A pipe used to carry discharge from sanitary fittings like bathrooms, kitchens etc. is called
explain: Waste pipes carry 'sullage'—water that does not contain human excreta.

q: 200. All anti-siphonage pipe is not required in
explain: A single stack system relies on a larger diameter pipe and carefully designed branches to prevent siphoning without needing a separate vent/anti-siphonage pipe.
